gloss: devastate, despoil; devastation, violence; Shaddai, the Almighty
summary: The verb is to deal violently with and lay waste: an army coming on a land, a city or a tent pulled down, a robber by night, a son who assaults his father (Jer 4:20; 48:8; Oba 1:5; Pro 19:26). Most of its uses are the prophets’ cry over the nations and Judah, and in them Yahweh himself “devastates” by the destroyers he sends (Jer 25:36; 51:53–55). שֹׁד is the devastation, and the violence men do, often paired with חָמָס (Jer 6:7; Ezk 45:9). שַׁדַּי, the name God gave himself to the fathers (Exo 6:3), is set beside שֹׁד twice: “as devastation from Shaddai it comes” (Isa 13:6; Joel 1:15); Job speaks of his arrows and his great power (Job 6:4; 37:23), and in Genesis El Shaddai is the God who makes fruitful. The letters שד also spell שַׁד “breast”, a separate older word (ṯd in Ugaritic and Arabic, where the verb is šdd), which Jacob’s blessing sets beside Shaddai in play (Gen 49:25).

words.summary: To fall on with violence and lay waste: almost always of an enemy’s onslaught on a land, a city, its people or its goods, and of Yahweh who sends it. The participle שֹׁדֵד “the destroyer, the despoiler” is a third of its uses.

senses.gloss: devastate, lay waste (a land, city, people)
senses.definition: Of an army or of Yahweh: to fall on a land, a city or a people and lay it waste. The participle שֹׁדֵד is “the destroyer” who comes on them, often suddenly.

evidence.note: “The day that is coming לִשְׁדוֹד all the Philistines, to cut off from Tyre and Sidon every helper that remains, for Yahweh is devastating (שֹׁדֵד) the Philistines.”

“The destroyer of Moab has come up against you; he has ruined (שִׁחֵת) your strongholds.”
“Arise, go up against Kedar, and devastate the sons of the east”: Nebuchadnezzar’s campaign.
The ruthless of the nations “will devastate the pride of Egypt, and all her multitude will be destroyed”.
The shepherds wail, “for Yahweh is devastating (שֹׁדֵד) their pasture”.
“Though Babylon should go up to the heavens … from me destroyers would come to her”, declares Yahweh.
“Yahweh is devastating Babylon.”
“From the north the destroyers will come to her.”
“A destroyer has come upon her, upon Babylon … for Yahweh is a God of recompenses.”
“Make mourning as for an only son, for suddenly the destroyer will come upon us”: the people from the north (Jer 6:22).
“On all the bare heights in the wilderness destroyers have come, for the sword of Yahweh devours.”
“I brought on the mother of young men a destroyer at noonday.”
On Moab’s summer fruit and vintage “a destroyer has fallen”.
“Be a hiding place for them from the destroyer”, beside the oppressor and the trampler.
“The betrayer betrays and the destroyer destroys: go up, Elam; besiege, Media.”
“And you, שָׁדוּד, devastated one, what will you do?”: Jerusalem, decking herself in vain.
“Daughter of Babylon, הַשְּׁדוּדָה”: the one to be devastated.
Sisera: “where he bowed, there he fell, שָׁדוּד”, undone, slain.
“Woe, destroyer, and you not destroyed! … When you finish destroying, you will be destroyed.”
The infinitive שָׁדוֹד with the niphal: “we are utterly devastated”.
“The cutting off that יָשׁוּד, lays waste, at noon”, beside the plague in darkness; spelled as from שׁוּד.

senses.gloss: despoil, rob; deal violently with (a person)
senses.definition: Of men against men: to fall on someone to rob or harm them. The שֹׁדְדִים are despoilers, set beside thieves.

Of the wicked: “in peace the destroyer comes upon him”.
“A wolf of the evenings will ravage them”: a beast of prey, of the enemy.

senses.definition: Once, with the qal infinitive, in the lament put in Israel’s mouth: their land taken and divided to others.

evidence.note: שָׁדוֹד נְשַׁדֻּנוּ, “we are utterly devastated; he changes the portion of my people … he divides our fields”.

senses.definition: To set upon a person or his home with violence.

evidence.note: מְשַׁדֶּד־אָב, “he who assaults his father and drives away his mother is a son who causes shame”.
“Do not lie in wait (תֶּאֱרֹב), wicked man, against the dwelling of the righteous; do not assault his resting place.”

senses.definition: The cry of the devastated land, city or people, nearly always in the prophets’ laments: “for it is devastated”.

evidence.note: “Breach upon breach is cried, for all the land is devastated; suddenly my tents are devastated, my curtains in a moment.”
“My tent is devastated and all my cords are broken; my sons have gone from me.”

שֻׁדַּד שָׂדֶה … שֻׁדַּד דָּגָן, “the field is laid waste … the grain is laid waste”: of the locust, with a play on שָׂדֶה.

“Wail, cypress, for the cedar has fallen, the majestic ones are laid waste.”

senses.definition: Once, of Yahweh breaking down Israel’s altars and pillars.

senses.definition: The passive יוּשַּׁד / תּוּשַּׁד, of the destroyer’s own end and of Israel’s fortresses.

senses.definition: Violent wrong done by people to others, the poor above all; nearly always paired with חָמָס and set against justice.

“As a well keeps its water fresh, so she keeps fresh her evil: חָמָס וָשֹׁד is heard in her.”
“They do not know how to do right … who store up חָמָס וָשֹׁד in their palaces.”
“שֹׁד and violence are before me; there is strife.”
“The violence done to Lebanon will cover you, and the שֹׁד of beasts will terrify them.”
“Because of the despoiling of the poor, the groaning of the needy, now I will arise, says Yahweh.”
“The violence of the wicked drags them away, for they refuse to do justice.”
“Their heart devises שֹׁד, and their lips speak trouble.”

words.gloss: Shaddai, the Almighty: a name of God
words.summary: A name of the God of Israel, 48 times, 31 of them in Job. In Genesis it is אֵל שַׁדַּי, the name by which he appeared to Abraham, Isaac and Jacob (Exo 6:3), always with the promise to make them fruitful and many. Elsewhere Shaddai is God in his overpowering might: his arrows, his wrath, his great power, the devastation of his day (Job 6:4; 21:20; 37:23; Isa 13:6). The database files it under שדה with “breast”; it is placed here because its doubled ד fits a root שדד, where “my breasts” is שָׁדַי without it (Sng 1:13), and because Isaiah and Joel set it beside this root’s שֹׁד. Jacob’s blessing plays on the other word (Gen 49:25). No verse explains the name, and no cognate gives it; the link to the root is a reading of the form and of these two plays.

senses.gloss: El Shaddai, the God of the fathers, who makes fruitful
senses.definition: The name in which God appeared to Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, making them his covenant and promise: to multiply them into nations and kings and give their seed the land.

evidence.note: “I am אֵל שַׁדַּי; walk before me and be whole, and I will give my covenant … and multiply you exceedingly” (17:1–2).
Isaac to Jacob: “אֵל שַׁדַּי bless you and make you fruitful and multiply you, that you may become an assembly of peoples.”
“I am אֵל שַׁדַּי: be fruitful and multiply; a nation and an assembly of nations will come from you, and kings from your loins.”
Jacob: “אֵל שַׁדַּי appeared to me at Luz and blessed me, and said, I will make you fruitful … and give this land to your seed” (48:3–4).
“May אֵל שַׁדַּי give you mercy before the man.”
“By the God of your father who helps you, and with Shaddai who blesses you … blessings of שָׁדַיִם and womb”: Shaddai set beside “breasts” in play.
“I appeared to Abraham, to Isaac and to Jacob בְּאֵל שַׁדָּי, but by my name Yahweh I was not known to them”; he had made his covenant with them to give them Canaan (6:4).
The sound of the cherubim’s wings “like the voice of אֵל־שַׁדַּי when he speaks”.

senses.gloss: Shaddai, the Almighty, in power and judgment
senses.definition: God as the one whose power none withstands: who brings calamity and devastation, whose arrows and wrath strike, and who is just in all he does; and so the one to fear and to trust, whose breath gives life and in whose shadow one is safe.

evidence.note: “The day of Yahweh is near; as שֹׁד from שַׁדַּי it comes”: devastation from the Devastator.
“Shaddai, we cannot find him out; great in power (שַׂגִּיא־כֹחַ), and in justice and abundant righteousness he does not oppress.”
“The arrows of Shaddai are in me; my spirit drinks their poison.”
“Call me Mara, for Shaddai has dealt very bitterly with me.”
“Yahweh has testified against me, and Shaddai has done evil (הֵרַע) to me.”
“Let him drink of the wrath of Shaddai.”
“As God lives, who has taken away my right, and Shaddai, who has embittered my soul.”
“God has made my heart faint; Shaddai has terrified me.”
“When Shaddai scattered kings there.”
The sound of the wings “like the sound of many waters, like the voice of Shaddai, … like the noise of a camp”.
“Does God pervert justice, or does Shaddai pervert righteousness?”
“Far be it from God to do wickedness, and from Shaddai to do wrong” (and 34:12).
“Do not despise the discipline of Shaddai.”
“The spirit of God made me, and the breath of Shaddai gives me life.”
“The breath of Shaddai gives them understanding.”
“He who dwells in the secret place of the Most High will lodge in the shadow of Shaddai.”
Balaam “sees the vision of Shaddai”, beside אֵל and (24:16) עֶלְיוֹן.
“Shaddai will be your gold.”
“Shall a faultfinder contend with Shaddai?”
“The war of that great day of God παντοκράτορος”: the day of Yahweh which Isa 13:6 and Joel 1:15 say comes “as devastation from Shaddai”.
“He treads the winepress of the fury of the wrath of God παντοκράτορος.”
“Says the Lord παντοκράτωρ”; in Revelation and here the title also stands for יַהְוֶה צְבָאוֹת, so it is a bridge, not a quotation of Shaddai.

parallels.note: God, in the other half of the line, through Job.
Naomi’s parallel: Yahweh testified against me, Shaddai did me evil.

words.summary: A woman’s breast, that gives suck; mostly dual, שָׁדַיִם. Also spelled שֹׁד. It shares its letters with שֹׁד “devastation” but not its older root: Ugaritic, Arabic and Aramaic give it ṯ (ṯd, ṯady, tdā), where the verb is Ugaritic šdd. It is kept here because the spelling is one and Jacob’s blessing sets it beside Shaddai (Gen 49:25).

senses.definition: The breast from which a child sucks, and so nursing and infancy; in the prophets, figured of Zion fed by the nations and comforted.

evidence.note: “Why did the knees receive me, and why שָׁדַיִם, that I should suck (אִינָק)?”

senses.definition: A woman’s breasts as the sign of her being grown, as the place of love, and, in the prophets’ figure, of Israel’s harlotry.

words.summary: Once, singular and plural together, among Qoheleth’s acquisitions; its meaning is not fixed by the text. Coming after male and female singers among “the delights of the sons of man”, and built like Deborah’s רַחַם רַחֲמָתַיִם, “a womb, two wombs” for each man (Jdg 5:30), it is most likely a woman of the king’s house, named from the breast. That link to שַׁד is a reading of the context, with no cognate to confirm it.

“How fair and pleasant you are, O love, among the delights (תַּעֲנוּגִים)”: the word Qoheleth uses before שִׁדָּה.

doctrine.statement: The verses name Yahweh himself as the one who devastates: “Yahweh is devastating their pasture”, “Yahweh is devastating the Philistines”, “Yahweh is devastating Babylon” (Jer 25:36; 47:4; 51:55). The destroyers who come are his: “from me destroyers will come to her” (Jer 51:53); they come because “the sword of Yahweh devours” (Jer 12:12); and his day comes “as devastation from Shaddai” (Isa 13:6; Joel 1:15). Naomi says the same of her own loss: “Shaddai has dealt bitterly with me … Shaddai has done evil to me” (Rut 1:20–21), as Yahweh says “I make peace and create evil” and Amos asks “shall there be evil in a city and Yahweh has not done it?” (Isa 45:7; Amo 3:6). So scripture knows no destroyer acting against God’s will: calamity on nations and on individuals comes from God, in judgment or in discipline (Job 5:17), and the human destroyer is the instrument he sends.

The destroyer is himself destroyed: “Woe, destroyer … when you finish destroying, you will be destroyed” (Isa 33:1). Babylon, which devastated Judah, is “the daughter of Babylon, to be devastated”, and “blessed is he who repays you what you did to us” (Psa 137:8); a destroyer comes on her, “for Yahweh is a God of recompenses; he will surely repay” (Jer 51:56), and the call is “repay her according to her work” (Jer 50:29). Revelation takes up the same words against the Babylon of its day: “Render to her as she rendered” (Rev 18:6). The verses show God measuring judgment to the deed: those who live by violence receive it back.

Each time El Shaddai speaks or is invoked in Genesis it is with the same promise: “I am El Shaddai … I will multiply you exceedingly” to Abraham; “El Shaddai bless you and make you fruitful and multiply you” over Jacob; “be fruitful and multiply; a nation and an assembly of nations … and kings”; and “I will make you fruitful … and give this land to your seed after you for an everlasting possession” (Gen 17:1–2; 28:3; 35:11; 48:3–4). In Exodus God says that he appeared to the fathers as El Shaddai and established his covenant with them to give them Canaan, and that as Yahweh he will now bring it to pass (Exo 6:3–4). The name of power in Job is the same name in which the promise of seed and land was given: the one able to make it good.

note: Drafted 2026-11-13 for Num 10:18–19, 25 (the Shaddai names). Root key שדד as the database keys the verb (v.bg.aa) and its noun שֹׁד (v.bg.ab). The database (after BDB) files שַׁדַּי (v.bh.af), שַׁד “breast” (v.bh.ab, with the duplicate key v.bh.ac carrying the same 30 tokens, not named), שִׁדָּה (v.bh.ae) and the name Shedeur (v.bh.ad, names/shedeur.json, entry or) under a root שדה; this entry takes them all, with root שדה on שַׁד and שִׁדָּה, so the entry answers to both keys. Judgment call for review: שַׁדַּי is put under שדד (no word root), on its doubled ד (שָׁדַי “my breasts” Sng 1:13 has none) and on the pun כְּשֹׁד מִשַּׁדַּי (Isa 13:6; Joel 1:15); Gen 49:25 puns on “breasts” instead. The breast word is a separate older root (ṯ) in the same letters, so its cognates are named on it alone; the verb’s š rests on Ugaritic yšdd (Segert p. 201, read from OCR “/8-d-d/”, which this scan uses for š; check the page image). Token overlap: the spelling שֹׁד makes the database count Isa 60:16; 66:11; Job 24:9 (breast) under v.bg.ab, and Hos 9:6; Amo 5:9; Hab 1:3; 2:17; Psa 12:6; Job 5:21 (devastation) under v.bh.ab; each verse is cited under the word it is. Zero-token cross-references v.bf.ae and v.bo.ad are put on the verb, v.bo.ac on שֹׁד, v.bf.ac on שַׁד. The forms יוּשַּׁד / תּוּשַּׁד (Isa 33:1; Hos 10:14), listed by the database as qal passive, are entered under hophal, the schema having no qal passive; Psa 91:6 יָשׁוּד is entered under the qal. Left out: שֵׁד “demon” (Deu 32:17; Psa 106:37; v.bf.ad, filed by the database under שגר), a loan from Akkadian šēdu “protective spirit” (Oracc armep x000018600), for an entry of its own; the place אַשְׁדּוֹד Ashdod (v.bg.ac, root אשד); שׂדד “harrow” and שִׂדִּים Siddim, spelled with sin. Arabic: the regular match for *šdd is سدّ “close up, stop a gap” (Lane p. 1328), which shares nothing with the Hebrew, so it is not recorded; شدّ is Hebrew שׂדד’s match. Not consulted: Ge’ez (Dillmann, Leslau) for sadada “drive out”; DULAT for Ugaritic šdd and ṯd; the Deir ʿAlla plaster text’s šdyn (gods called Shaddayin), the only extra-biblical Northwest Semitic use of the name, which is not in sources.json. The Peshitta has no word of the root. Names formed from שַׁדַּי: Ammishaddai (names/ammishaddai.json), Zurishaddai (names/zurishaddai.json, entry tsur), Shedeur (names/shedeur.json, entry or). The doctrine ‘yahweh-sends-calamity’ states the reading that no destroyer acts apart from God (Isa 45:7); review.
